5.0.0.en: By birth Reuben is considered the firstborn, but he committed a great sin, which was his adultery with his father's wife, that is, his concubine or maidservant whom he had taken as a wife. Therefore the birthright, with its honor and its blessing, was taken from him and given to Joseph because of his godliness from his youth, then his love for his brothers, his forbearance with them, his forgiveness of them, his hosting them in Egypt and his care for them. So God gave him a double portion beyond his brothers, in that his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh each received the portion of a tribe in the land, that is, double, and not the portion of one tribe only. God wishes to declare here that the blessing is given to the one who fears Him and is taken from the one who makes light of His word.

5.0.1.en: Hold fast to God's commandments, that you may enjoy His care, His love and His blessings in your life. Every struggle you undertake is very precious to God, even if it is a cup of cold water, and God wants to reward you, so show your love for Him.

5.1.1.en: Here he points to the standing of the tribe of Judah, because from its descendants came Christ, the Author of our salvation and our Redeemer. Judah, then, has his standing, but the blessing went to Joseph because of his godliness. Because of the honor and importance of the tribe of Judah, he mentioned its genealogy at the beginning of this book, so as to arrive at King David, from whom Christ comes (chs. 2-4).

5.2.s.en: (2) The genealogies of the tribe of Reuben

5.2.0.en: Tilgath-pilneser: he is the same as Tiglath-pileser (2 Kgs 15:29), the Assyrian king who carried away the kingdom of Israel into captivity.

5.2.1.en: Here he mentions the genealogies of the tribe of Reuben, beginning with Reuben and continuing to the Assyrian captivity in 722 BC. The tribe of Reuben was carried into captivity before the other tribes because it dwelt east of the Jordan River, that is, facing Assyria, which lay to the east of the land of the Jews. The span of time between the life of Reuben and the Assyrian captivity is about 1100 years, and it is therefore understood that the writer of this book did not mention all the genealogies of Reuben but abridged them, because of their lack of importance.

5.2.2.en: Hezron and Carmi, sons of Reuben, are not the ones mentioned in (ch. 2) among the descendants of Judah.

5.3.0.en: He continues the account of the descendants of Reuben, and mentions that they dwelt from Aroer to the region of Nebo, which is one of the peaks of the Jearim mountain range, and to the city of Baal-meon. All of these were cities and places that the tribe of Reuben possessed, east of the Jordan River and east of the Dead Sea. Moses went up Mount Nebo to see the land of Canaan, which God had promised to His people, before he died.

5.3.1.en: The registration by genealogy mentioned here means the one that took place in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel.

5.4.0.en: The tribe of Reuben was concerned to possess the fertile lands east of the Jordan River, even as far as the Euphrates River, which is in present-day Iraq. These regions are fertile pastures suitable for the livestock of the tribe of Reuben, and thus God's promise that the children of Israel would possess the land from the Euphrates to the river of Egypt is fulfilled. Reuben was not concerned to drive out the wicked in the regions neighboring him, but was concerned for the fertile land, which in time made him negligent and caused him to mingle with the wicked around him and to worship their gods. In choosing the fertile places and neglecting spiritual things he is like Lot, and he lost much, for he was the first of the tribes to be carried into captivity. He was not like Abraham, the father of the fathers, who obeyed God and lived in the wilderness, nor like Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who was concerned to possess the city of Hebron in the land of Canaan.

5.4.1.en: Be concerned for your spiritual goal, which is life with Christ and your place in the Kingdom, before your material ambitions, because the love of possessions hinders you and occupies your heart away from the love of God.

5.5.0.en: The Hagarites: probably the descendants of Hagar, that is, the descendants of Ishmael.

5.5.1.en: Gilead: the region lying east of the Jordan River. Its western part is fertile, while its eastern part is desert, and most of the land of Gilead lies in the portion of the tribe of Gad.

5.5.2.en: The book tells us that the descendants of Reuben waged war against the Hagarites in order to take their places, and they prevailed over them and took possession of their tents. This was in the days of Saul, the first of the kings of the children of Israel.

5.6.s.en: (3) The genealogies of the tribe of Gad

5.6.0.en: Bashan: a fertile region lying northeast of the Jordan River, reaching northward to the sources of the river, and famous for its oak trees.

5.6.1.en: Salchah: a fertile region lying east of Bashan.

5.6.2.en: The descendants of Gad dwelt north of the descendants of Reuben and settled in the region of Bashan, as far as Salchah, which was within the eastern borders of the kingdom of the children of Israel.

5.7.0.en: Sharon: a fertile region lying east of the Jordan River, which is different from the Sharon that lies west of the Jordan River toward the Mediterranean Sea.

5.7.1.en: Here he mentions some of the descendants of Gad, those who lived in the days of the Assyrian captivity, in order to make clear that it was because of their sins that they went into captivity (2 Kgs 15:29).

5.8.0.en: This shows the concern of the descendants of Gad to record their names in the genealogy, which was made in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam II king of Israel.

5.8.1.en: It is good for you to know your lineage, that you are a Christian, a son of the King of kings and Lord of lords, so that you do not become lax toward evil desires, but learn that you are the head of all creation, to lead it in praising and thanking God. Do not be distracted from your prayer, so that you may always live in purity.

5.9.0.en: Here he tells us in detail of the war that took place between the children of Israel and the Hagarites. The people of God who dwelt east of the Jordan River gathered, namely the men of the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh. Their number was great, 44,760, and they were men trained for war with swords, shields, bows and all the instruments of war.

5.10.0.en: The people of God set out to fight a group of tribes, all of them descendants of Ishmael, who dwelt in Gilead, in its eastern region.

5.11.0.en: The book makes clear the secret of the victory of the people of God over the Hagarites, which was their prayer and their trust in God; by the power of God they prevailed over them.

5.11.1.en: If you trust in God, be sure that you are able to overcome all the armies of the demons, because they are nothing before His power, however great your weakness. Do not be troubled by the multitude of your falls, but be strong in faith and seek God in humility, confident that by His power you are able to triumph over all your sins.

5.12.0.en: God's blessing is shown in the abundance of spoil that His people gained from their war with the Hagarites, and likewise in the vast numbers of captives.

5.13.0.en: It is evident from this verse that the war was severe, and the people of God killed a great number of the descendants of Ishmael. The victory depended on God's presence with His people; although they were trained for war and their number was great, their reliance was on God. They took possession of their lands and dwelt in them, but sadly they did not continue in purity of heart and in their worship of God, so God allowed them to be carried into captivity, that they might repent and return to Him once again.

6.0.0.en: The book tells us about the descendants of Levi in order to arrive at the priests, whose head is Aaron, the grandson of Kohath the son of Levi.

6.0.1.en: Amram begot three children: Moses, Aaron and Miriam. Moses is the leader and chief who delivered his people, Aaron is the high priest, and Miriam is the prophetess. Thus Levi begot deliverance, the priesthood and prophecy, and all of these are united in Christ, for they are types of Him.

6.0.2.en: Aaron begot four sons, two of whom, Nadab and Abihu, died without offspring because they offered strange fire, and so they represent the punishment of disobedience.

6.0.3.en: Eleazar is the priest whom the grace of God chose, and from his descendants came Jehozadak, who went into captivity, and then his grandson Jeshua, who returned from the captivity and served as priest in the house that he built with Zerubbabel (Hag 1:1). After that the priestly lineage became obscure for more than 300 years, until Christ the Great High Priest was born.

6.0.4.en: As for Ithamar, his descendants were excluded from the priesthood because of their evils. Among them were Eli the priest and his son Phinehas, and the last of them was Abiathar, whom King Solomon removed.

6.1.0.en: The book mentions the descendants of Aaron until it reaches Ahitub, who was a priest in the days of Saul, the first of the kings of the children of Israel. It is noted that it does not mention all the descendants, because the time between Levi and the return from the captivity is about 1300 years, so that it includes far more than the names written in this genealogy; it has omitted many because of their lack of importance.

6.2.0.en: In this sequence it mentions Zadok, who was high priest in the days of David, and his son Ahimaaz, who gave warning of the conspiracy of Absalom and saved David from death.

6.2.1.en: The Johanan mentioned here is probably Jehoiada, who preserved King Joash and raised him, until he anointed him king at the age of seven over the kingdom of Judah (2 Kgs 11:4).

6.3.0.en: This Azariah is probably the high priest who tried to prevent King Uzziah from entering the house of the Lord to burn incense; and since the king refused, God struck him with leprosy because of his presumption against the priesthood and his disobedience to Azariah the high priest (2 Chr 26:17-20). Here the godly high priests appear: Jehoiada protects the blessed offspring Joash from the evil of Queen Athaliah, and Azariah shows his holy zeal for the house of God, as he tries to prevent the king from presuming against the priesthood.

6.3.1.en: Be faithful in carrying out your responsibilities, whatever dangers you may meet, because God is with you, protecting you, guiding you and supporting you, as He was with the godly men in every generation.

6.4.0.en: Here in the genealogies of Aaron we see names repeated for other persons, such as the repetition of the names Ahitub and Zadok, who are different from those who lived in the days of Saul and David.

6.4.1.en: At the end of this sequence we see Jehozadak the high priest, who lived in the days of the Babylonian captivity and went away with the captives. As for his father Seraiah the high priest, Nebuchadnezzar killed him at the attack on Jerusalem. We notice that Eleazar the high priest, the son of Aaron, came out of the bondage of Egypt and was established as a priest in the wilderness of Sinai, while Jehozadak his descendant went out from Jerusalem into the bondage of captivity, and this was because of the negligence and evil of the people of God and its priests. God saves His children from afflictions, but because of their sins they need His discipline once again.

13.0.s.en: (5) The mighty men from all the tribes at Hebron to make David king

13.0.0.en: This part, mentioned here from (vv. 1-5), was referred to by the Second Book of Samuel in (2 Sam 6:

13.0.1.en: 1), that is, it mentioned it briefly, whereas here he explains to us the details of the event, which is that after David became king over all Israel, he thought before everything else of bringing the ark of the covenant of the Lord to Jerusalem, so that his throne might be beside the ark. The gathering of the people around God, represented in the ark of His covenant, came before their gathering around the king, and this shows David's humility, his faith and his submission to God.

13.0.2.en: So he gathered the commanders of his army and the heads of the tribes, that is, all those in authority in Israel, and consulted them about moving the ark of the covenant of God from the city of Jearim to Jerusalem. He did this so that the tribes would not be displeased at the presence of the ark within the kingdom of Judah beside the king, but that it might be with their counsel and agreement, and this shows David's wisdom and his concern to please all the tribes.

13.0.3.en: The people of God had been divided into thousands and hundreds since the days of Moses (Num 31:14, Deut 1:15), to make it easy to lead them and to convey news to them. So David gathered the captains of thousands and captains of hundreds, because they represent the whole people, in order to take with them a political and administrative decision, which was the moving of the ark, and he summoned the priests, as we shall see in the following verses, because it was at the same time a religious act.

13.1.0.en: Their suburbs: the areas surrounding the cities of the Levites, used for pasturing sheep, extending two thousand cubits around the city in which they dwell.

13.1.1.en: David spoke with the heads of the tribes of Israel, who represent all the people of God, and he spoke to them concerning bringing up the ark of the covenant of God and moving it from the place where it was, the city of Jearim, to Jerusalem, where David reigns. In this he wished to gather all the peoples around God, represented in the ark of His covenant, and not around himself as their king. And he said two things to them:

13.1.2.en: 1- "If it seem good unto you," that is, if you agree to this. This shows his kindness, his humility and his concern to please his people.

13.1.3.en: 2- "And that it be of the Lord our God," that is, David's concern for the mind of God, before whom he prays that he may hear His voice; only then would he move the ark. The mind of God was more important to David than anything else; therefore he prayed first, before speaking to the heads of Israel.

13.1.4.en: David asked the leaders to send word to all the people in their places, that they might come and bring up the ark of the covenant of God. He says "bring up" because Jerusalem is built on five hills.

13.1.5.en: David stressed the summoning of the priests and the Levites, because they are the servants of God who would carry the ark and minister to it.

13.1.6.en: We notice David's love and humility in calling the people his brethren, and he did not exalt himself over them as a king. He is a type of Christ, who calls those who believe in Him His brethren (Heb 2:11). We also see that the priests and the Levites had been scattered throughout all the land of Israel, because the service of the ark had ceased since the days of Eli the priest, when the Philistines took the ark and then sent it back, and it remained for a time in the city of Jearim.

13.2.0.en: David felt the sin of the people of God, that they had forgotten the ark of the covenant of God throughout the days of Saul's reign, because of Saul's distance from God. But David's humility and sense of responsibility made him ascribe the fault to himself and to all the people, so that he said "we enquired not." Humility made David ascribe the fault to himself and not condemn others.

13.2.1.en: May you turn the blame upon yourself when mistakes occur in which you shared with others, and not incline to condemnation, because your repentance and humility bring upon you the mercies of God, while your condemnation brings upon you the wrath of God and His judgment.

13.2.2.en: David said, "let us bring again the ark of our God," because the ark had been set down at the beginning of the entrance of the people of God into the Promised Land, at Gilgal (Josh 5:10), for a short time in the days of Joshua, and then was moved to Shiloh (1 Sam 1:3) and remained there about three hundred years, until the days of Samuel. After that the Philistines took it (1 Sam 5), when they triumphed over the children of Israel, and they were struck with many diseases, so they sent the ark to Beth-shemesh (1 Sam 6:12), a Jewish city, but the people were not careful in approaching the ark, and fifty thousand of them died, so they moved it to the city of Jearim (1 Sam 7:1), and it remained there throughout the reign of Saul. The ark alone was moved to these places, from the Philistines to Beth Shemesh to Jearim, while the remaining parts of the tabernacle of meeting were moved from Shiloh to the city of Nob and remained there throughout the days of Saul. The separation of the ark from the tabernacle was temporary, from the time the Philistines took it until it returned again in the days of Solomon, when he placed it in the Temple.

13.3.0.en: The leaders obeyed David's word and informed the people in their cities of the intention to bring up the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and the people agreed, and even showed their concern for this matter. The leaders informed David of the readiness of all to carry out what he had proposed. This shows the love of the leaders and the people for God, and so they agreed and obeyed their king readily.

13.4.0.en: Shihor: a word meaning black, and it is meant to refer to the Nile of Egypt, which carries silt; probably there was a branch of the Nile extending into the desert of Sinai, and this is what is meant by Shihor.

13.4.1.en: Hamath: a city lying north of Damascus, at a distance of 190 km north of Damascus.

13.4.2.en: Jearim: a village lying on the border between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, north of Jerusalem, at a distance of 14 km.

13.4.3.en: David gathered the people of the children of Israel from the farthest reaches of their land, that is, beside the desert of Sinai and the river Shihor, to the farthest north, that is, beside Hamath, and they all moved to the city of Jearim to bring the ark of the covenant of God from it to Jerusalem.

13.4.5.en: 6- And David went up, and all Israel, to Baalah, that is, to Kirjathjearim, which belonged to Judah, to bring up thence the ark of God the Lord, that dwelleth between the cherubims, whose name is called on it. 7- And they carried the ark of God in a new cart out of the house of Abinadab: and Uzza and Ahio drave the cart. 8- And David and all Israel played before God with all their might, and with singing, and with harps, and with psalteries, and with timbrels, and with cymbals, and with trumpets. 9- And when they came unto the threshingfloor of Chidon, Uzza put forth his hand to hold the ark; for the oxen stumbled. 10- And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzza, and he smote him, because he put forth his hand to the ark: and there he died before God. 11- And David was displeased, because the Lord had made a breach upon Uzza: wherefore that place is called Perezuzza to this day.

13.4.6.en: These events were recorded in the text in (2 Sam 6:2-8) and were explained in the book al-Mawsu'a (the Encyclopedia), Part Five. In summary, David erred in that he placed the ark on two oxen, contrary to the Law, which requires that only the priests carry it. Despite his joy and the joy of all the people and his proud dancing to the sound of the music, God declared His anger through the rushing of the oxen, until the ark was in danger of falling to the ground. Then Uzza the son of Abinadab, who served the ark in his father's house, rushed forward and stretched out his hand and touched the ark, and fell dead at once, because no man is permitted to touch the ark. So David grieved over the death of Uzza, and he forgot his own error in imitating the Philistines, who placed the ark on a new cart drawn by two cows. But the Philistines had their excuse, since they were pagans who did not know the Law of God, whereas David knew the Law and how the ark was to be carried, as God had commanded.

13.4.7.en: It also reminds us that before the ark His name was called upon, that is, the people of God worshiped Him and called upon His name and did not mention strange gods, because the ark represents the presence of God.

13.4.8.en: David rejoiced at bringing back the ark, but he did not obey the Law of God concerning how to move the ark, and so God was angry. May you, when you pray and praise and do works of goodness to rejoice the heart of God, be concerned to obey His commandments and all that the Church teaches, that you may pray and serve in the way God wants, and not imitate the people of the world, for you are different from them; for when David imitated the Philistines in moving the ark, God was angry.

13.4.9.en: (3) The blessing of the house of Obed-edom (vv. 12-14:)

13.4.10.en: 12- And David was afraid of God that day, saying, How shall I bring the ark of God home to me? 13- So David brought not the ark home to himself to the city of David, but carried it aside into the house of Obededom the Gittite. 14- And the ark of God remained with the family of Obededom in his house three months. And the Lord blessed the house of Obededom, and all that he had. These verses were explained previously in (2 Sam 6:9-11), and in summary what happened was David's fear of God when He struck Uzza, so he placed the ark in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months and did not move it to Jerusalem.

13.4.11.en: When you fear God, this calls you to keep away from sin and not from God, because He makes you afraid so that you may keep away from evil, but He has compassion on you with His care and His fatherhood and satisfies you. So when you sin, do not withdraw from Him in shame, but stand before Him in prayer and prostrate yourself in His presence, offering repentance, and you will obtain His mercies and forgiveness.

13.4.12.en: The First Book of Kings: King David became great
